2	
3	We introduced a formal diagnostic framework---episode-level counterfactual analysis with the DAF metric---for decomposing routing signal in modular LLM agents. 4	
5	Cross-domain contrasts demonstrate framework applicability: on MATH ($N{=}300$), death-avoidance signal is absent as predicted ($+4.3$~pp, $p = 0.079$, underpowered at 0.42); a Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct pilot (7 task types, 70 episodes) confirms directional consistency ($+34.3\%$ vs.\ $+26.6\%$). 1	\section{Related Work}
2	
3	\paragraph{Tool Use and External Computation in LLMs.}
4	A growing body of work augments language models with external tools \citep{tool-learning-survey-2024}.
5	Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches LLMs to insert API calls via self-supervised loss filtering; ToolkenGPT \cite{toolkengpt-2023} represents tools as special tokens enabling frozen models to invoke massive tool libraries; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} composes heterogeneous modules per subtask; ReTool \cite{retool-2025} applies RL to discover when code execution is preferable to chain-of-thought.
6	These focus on \emph{learning to use tools}; we ask a prior question: \emph{what signal drives the routing decision?}
7	Recent concurrent work sharpens this question: \citet{tool-overuse-illusion-2026} identify a cognitive-illusion effect in LLM tool use, \citet{when2tool-2026} show tool-call decisions are encoded in hidden states before reasoning, \citet{tool-use-tax-2026} quantify a ``tool-use tax'' where tools degrade performance, and \citet{to-call-or-not-2026} propose a necessity--utility--affordability framework.
8	Our counterfactual decomposition provides environment-grounded evidence: in ScienceWorld, $90.4\%$ of routing signal at $P{=}100$ traces to catastrophic-failure prevention.
9	
10	\paragraph{Adaptive Computation and Routing.}
11	CogRouter \cite{cogrouter-2026} adapts reasoning depth per step, ARES \cite{ares-2026} selects among reasoning effort levels, Mixture-of-Recursions \cite{mixture-of-recursions-2025} learns token-level recursion depths, and MTRouter \cite{mtrouter-2026} addresses multi-turn routing across heterogeneous models.
12	RouteLLM \citep{routellm-2024} learns routers from preference data to select between strong and weak models.
13	These optimize \emph{how} to route; we reveal \emph{why} routing helps---in interactive environments, the dominant signal is catastrophic-failure avoidance.
14	
15	\paragraph{Counterfactual Evaluation in RL.}
16	Prior work generates counterfactual explanations for RL agents by perturbing individual actions within a fixed policy \citep{olson2021counterfactual, gajcin2023counterfactual, amitai2024explaining}.
17	Our approach differs in both purpose and granularity: we execute two complete episodes under different routing strategies, producing prospective paired comparisons that isolate routing signal \emph{before} any router is trained, sidestepping compounding perturbation artifacts.
18	
19	\paragraph{Safe RL and Catastrophic Failure.}
20	\citet{garcia2015comprehensive} survey safe RL methods that constrain policies to avoid catastrophic outcomes; \citet{crpo-2021} develop principled constrained optimization with formal convergence guarantees.
21	Our counterfactual decomposition reveals that death avoidance is the dominant component of routing signal, suggesting that modality routing functions primarily as a safety mechanism rather than a generic capability-matching problem.
22	
23	\paragraph{LLM Agents in Interactive Environments.}
24	ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022} serves as our primary testbed; ALFWorld \cite{alfworld-2021} provides a complementary household environment; AgentBench \cite{agentbench-2024} offers systematic evaluation across diverse interactive environments; Voyager \cite{voyager-2023} demonstrates open-ended exploration in Minecraft.
25	ReAct \cite{react-2023} interleaves reasoning with actions and serves as our internal baseline; Reflexion \cite{reflexion-2023} extends this with verbal self-reflection; LATS \cite{lats-2024} unifies reasoning, acting, and planning via tree search.
26	Hallucination detection methods such as SelfCheckGPT \cite{selfcheckgpt-2023} identify when LLM outputs are unreliable; our work shows that in interactive environments, such unreliability manifests as catastrophic agent death.
27	Our deterministic modality provides exact state transitions, and our analysis shows this exactness matters almost exclusively for death avoidance.
28

Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.
Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.
More recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}.
The shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources---accuracy, latency, capability matching---and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.
But this assumption has never been systematically verified: \emph{what actually drives the value of routing decisions in interactive environments?}

We propose a \emph{formal diagnostic framework} for answering this question. The framework comprises (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), a metric that decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\S\ref{sec:daf}). The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic agent death (a $-100$ penalty), while the deterministic strategy survives the same episodes.
Once death episodes are removed, the performance gap between strategies collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$.

The standard approach to generating routing labels---per-step oracle comparison---degenerates under sparse rewards.
In ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, leaving no step-level signal to learn from (\S\ref{sec:collection}).

    \item \textbf{Death avoidance dominance.}

The score-level DAF metric reaches $90.4\%$ at $P{=}100$ ($P$-dependent) but varies substantially across penalty settings. An exploratory router trained on these labels fails to outperform the trivial always-deterministic baseline on held-out episodes ($47.1 \pm 2.2\%$ vs.\ $50.0\%$); data scaling ablations confirm this capacity-dependent limitation; scaling to 4B yields $59.0\%$ episode-level accuracy but the cost (4B parameters for $+9$\,pp above random) is disproportionate when DAF $= 90.4\%$ and always-deterministic is trivially near-optimal (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

    \item \textbf{Cross-context applicability.}
    On MATH ($N{=}300$), where no death penalty exists, internal reasoning directionally outperforms code interpretation ($+4.3$~pp, $p = 0.079$, not reaching $\alpha{=}0.05$), consistent with the framework's prediction that death-avoidance signal should be absent without catastrophic failure. At episode level, the router performs below chance across all 8 seeds (range: 43.1\%--49.6\%). Augmentation-based data scaling (Table~\ref{tab:data-scaling}) from 25\% to 800\% ($32{\times}$ range) provides no improvement, converging to the always-deterministic baseline ($50\%$). However, paraphrase augmentation inflates the majority class without generating novel routing patterns; real-data scaling remains an open question. With DAF $= 90.4\%$ and all task types deterministic-majority (86:9 label ratio), always-deterministic trivially solves the episode-level routing problem, leaving no learnable signal for a step-level router.

\paragraph{Data scaling ablation.} To test whether the episode-level generalization failure stems from data scarcity, we vary training set size from 25\% to 800\% of the original via paraphrase-based data augmentation (synonym substitution + template variation on step observations), holding the episode-level validation set fixed. Table~\ref{tab:data-scaling} reports the results.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}rccc@{}}
\toprule
Scale & Samples & Det\% & Ep.\ Bal.\ Acc.\ (\%) \\
\midrule
25\% & 433 & ${\sim}90$ & $49.5 \pm 0.3$ \\
50\% & 867 & ${\sim}90$ & $51.5$ \\
100\% & 1{,}735 & 89.6 & $49.9 \pm 0.1$ \\
200\% & 3{,}470 & 94.2 & $50.0 \pm 0.0$ \\
800\% & 13{,}880 & ${\sim}97.7$ & $51.0 \pm 1.1$ \\
\midrule
Always-det & --- & --- & 50.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Data scaling ablation: episode-level balanced accuracy across training set sizes (25\%--800\% of original, $32{\times}$ range). Internal recall $= 0.0$ at all scales (complete majority-class collapse). Det\%: fraction of deterministic-preferred labels in training data. The 50\% scale is a single seed; all others report mean$\pm$std across seeds.}
\label{tab:data-scaling}
\end{table}

All scales hover at ${\sim}50\%$ episode-level balanced accuracy---equivalent to the always-deterministic baseline---with no monotonic improvement as data increases. Augmentation-based scaling provides no improvement at any scale; however, episode-level minority-class diversity remains a potential confound that cannot be resolved without collecting more internal-preferred episodes. The ground-truth internal-preferred rate (9/245 $= 3.7\%$) means collecting 50 internal-preferred episodes would require approximately 1{,}350 paired episodes at current environment dynamics---a $5.5{\times}$ expansion with diminishing return on a $9.6\%$ signal. The failure points instead to a structural limitation: when DAF $= 90.4\%$ and all task types are deterministic-majority (86:9 label ratio), the episode-level routing problem is trivially solved by always choosing deterministic, leaving no learnable signal for a step-level router to exploit.

"""Death rate measurement for Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on ScienceWorld."""
import argparse, json, os, sys, time, random

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "src"))
from scienceworld_utils import (
    create_env, reset_env, get_valid_actions, get_score,
    step_env, close_env, get_task_types, get_max_variations,
)
from llm_agent import LLMAgent

DEATH_THRESHOLD = -100

def run_episode_internal(agent, task_name, variation_idx, max_steps):
    env = create_env(task_name, variation_idx)
    obs, _ = reset_env(env)
    initial_score = get_score(env)
    action_history = []
    history_dicts = []
    t0 = time.time()

    for step_idx in range(max_steps):
        valid_actions = get_valid_actions(env)
        if not valid_actions:
            break
        action, raw = agent.select_action_react(obs, valid_actions, history_dicts)
        score_before = get_score(env)
        obs_new, reward, done, info = step_env(env, action)
        score_after = get_score(env)
        action_history.append(action)
        history_dicts.append({"action": action, "observation": obs_new[:200], "score": score_after})
        obs = obs_new
        if done:
            break

    final_score = get_score(env)
    close_env(env)
    death = final_score <= DEATH_THRESHOLD
    return {
        "task_name": task_name,
        "variation_idx": variation_idx,
        "final_score": final_score,
        "num_steps": len(action_history),
        "death": death,
        "time_s": round(time.time() - t0, 1),
    }

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--model_path", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--task_types", type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--episodes", type=int, default=5)
    parser.add_argument("--max_steps", type=int, default=30)
    parser.add_argument("--gpu_id", type=int, default=0)
    parser.add_argument("--output", type=str, default="guided_router/scaling_death_rate_0.5b.json")
    parser.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    random.seed(args.seed)
    task_names = [t.strip() for t in args.task_types.split(",")]

    available = get_task_types()
    resolved = []
    for t in task_names:
        if t in available:
            resolved.append(t)
        else:
            matches = [a for a in available if t.lower() in a.lower()]
            if matches:
                resolved.append(matches[0])
                print(f"Resolved '{t}' -> '{matches[0]}'")
            else:
                print(f"WARNING: task '{t}' not found, skipping")
    task_names = resolved
    print(f"Tasks to run: {task_names}")

    from episode_level_collection import cleanup_gpu_processes
    cleanup_gpu_processes(args.gpu_id)

    agent = LLMAgent(model_path=args.model_path, use_vllm=True, gpu_id=args.gpu_id)

    results = []
    for task_name in task_names:
        max_var = get_max_variations(task_name)
        for ep in range(args.episodes):
            var_idx = ep % max_var
            print(f"[{task_name}] Episode {ep+1}/{args.episodes} (var={var_idx})...", end=" ", flush=True)
            try:
                r = run_episode_internal(agent, task_name, var_idx, args.max_steps)
                r["episode"] = ep
                results.append(r)
                status = "DEATH" if r["death"] else f"score={r['final_score']:.1f}"
                print(f"{status} ({r['num_steps']} steps, {r['time_s']}s)")
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"ERROR: {e}")
                results.append({
                    "task_name": task_name, "episode": ep, "variation_idx": var_idx,
                    "final_score": -999, "death": True, "error": str(e),
                    "num_steps": 0, "time_s": 0,
                })

            os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(args.output) if os.path.dirname(args.output) else ".", exist_ok=True)
            with open(args.output, "w") as f:
                json.dump(results, f, indent=2)

    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("DEATH RATE SUMMARY: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct")
    print("="*60)

    all_deaths = sum(1 for r in results if r["death"])
    all_total = len(results)

    hypothesis = "supports" if delta > 0 else "contradicts"
    print(f"Conclusion: {hypothesis} 'smaller model -> higher death rate' hypothesis")

\section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}---a text-based science simulation with 30 task types---faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.
Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.
More recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}.
The shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources---accuracy, latency, capability matching---and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.
But this assumption has never been systematically verified: \emph{what actually drives the value of routing decisions in interactive environments?}

We propose a \emph{formal diagnostic framework} for answering this question. The framework comprises (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), a metric that decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\S\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, the framework reveals a surprisingly concentrated answer: \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95, penalty-independent); under ScienceWorld's default penalty ($P{=}100$), this corresponds to DAF $= 90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$).
The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic agent death (a $-100$ penalty), while the deterministic strategy survives the same episodes.
Once death episodes are removed, the performance gap between strategies collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$.

This framework addresses a methodological gap.
The standard approach to generating routing labels---per-step oracle comparison---degenerates under sparse rewards.
In ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, leaving no step-level signal to learn from (\S\ref{sec:collection}).
Keyword-based heuristics also fail structurally, as ScienceWorld actions lack science-specific terminology (\S\ref{sec:baselines}).
Our counterfactual approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, then compares episode outcomes to generate routing labels (\S\ref{sec:collection}). The framework is applicable to any environment with controllable modality comparison and binary catastrophic outcomes, requiring only paired episode outcomes under two modalities.

Our prescreening selected task types showing \emph{any} modality difference (not death-specific); the finding that 19 of 30 task types show no routing signal itself confirms signal sparsity. Among the 11 selected types (245 episode pairs), the full deterministic advantage is $\Delta_{\text{full}} = +29.60$ points.
Excluding death episodes, the gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$; 78.9\% of non-tie labels (75 of 95) arise from death asymmetry---a penalty-independent measure.
The penalty-sensitive Death Avoidance Factor (DAF; \S\ref{sec:daf}) is $90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$) at the default penalty $P{=}100$, ranging from 50\% ($P{=}10$) to 98\% ($P{=}500$).
The per-task correlation between death-rate differential and performance gap is $r = 0.97$ ($p < 10^{-6}$, $n = 11$), though this is largely a mathematical consequence of death dominance (partial $r = 0.02$, $p = 0.91$ after controlling for $\delta \cdot P$); we retain it as an internal consistency check (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}).

Two cross-context checks probe the specificity of this finding.
First, a MATH Level~4--5 evaluation (300 problems), using a code interpreter as the deterministic modality, shows a directional trend consistent with the absence of death-driven routing signal: internal reasoning outperforms code interpreter by $+4.3$~pp ($p = 0.079$, not reaching $\alpha{=}0.05$)---the opposite direction from ScienceWorld.
In the absence of death risk, the deterministic advantage is not statistically detectable ($p = 0.079$, not reaching $\alpha{=}0.05$).
Second, a cross-model replication with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (7 task types, 70 episode pairs) shows direction-consistent death patterns for all task types, with a larger death-rate differential ($+34.3\%$ vs.\ $+26.6\%$ for Qwen; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model}), confirming the phenomenon generalizes across model families.
An exploratory step-level router (Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA) trained on these counterfactual labels achieves $54.1 \pm 5.4\%$ step-level balanced accuracy but only $47.1 \pm 2.2\%$ on held-out episodes---below the always-deterministic baseline---a capacity-dependent limitation confirmed by data scaling ($32{\times}$) ablations; the 4B scale yields $59.0\%$ but the cost is disproportionate to the routing benefit (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{A formal diagnostic framework for routing signal decomposition.}
    We formalize episode-level counterfactual labeling (Algorithm~\ref{alg:labeling}) with the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF) metric, providing a general methodology applicable to environments with controllable modality comparison for quantifying what fraction of routing signal derives from catastrophic-failure avoidance versus non-death performance differences (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:daf}).

    \item \textbf{Death avoidance dominance.}
    On ScienceWorld, 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels stem from death asymmetry (label-level, penalty-independent). The score-level DAF metric reaches $90.4\%$ at $P{=}100$ ($P$-dependent) but varies substantially across penalty settings. An exploratory router trained on these labels fails to outperform the trivial always-deterministic baseline on held-out episodes ($47.1 \pm 2.2\%$ vs.\ $50.0\%$); data scaling ablations confirm this capacity-dependent limitation; scaling to 4B yields $59.0\%$ episode-level accuracy but the cost (4B parameters for $+9$\,pp above random) is disproportionate when DAF $= 90.4\%$ and always-deterministic is trivially near-optimal (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

    \item \textbf{Cross-context applicability.}
    On MATH ($N{=}300$), where no death penalty exists, internal reasoning directionally outperforms code interpretation ($+4.3$~pp, $p = 0.079$, not reaching $\alpha{=}0.05$), consistent with the framework's prediction that death-avoidance signal should be absent without catastrophic failure. On ALFWorld ($N{=}135$), the framework identifies a qualitatively different mechanism: information asymmetry (access to admissible actions) rather than death avoidance (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). True quantitative replication requires a second environment with catastrophic failure (e.g., NetHack, Crafter).
\end{enumerate}
